## Why a joint smoother?

The syntax

``` r
f(x1, x2, x3, x4)
```

defines one joint tensor-product GeDS spline. It is different from the additive model

``` r
f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4)
```

because the joint smoother can represent interactions among the covariates. This vignette uses joint smoothers with `NGeDS`, `GGeDS`, and `NGeDSboost`, and compares them with additive `NGeDSgam` and `NGeDSboost` models. Joint smoothers use the SR stopping rule by default; the additive one-dimensional `NGeDS` learners use RD. `GGeDS` uses SR by default.

```{r}
library("GeDS")

wiggly4 <- function(x1, x2, x3, x4) {
  g <- function(x) {
    exp(-50 * (x - 0.3)^2) + 0.6 * exp(-80 * (x - 0.75)^2)
  }
  3 * g(x1) * g(x2) * (0.5 + x3) * (0.5 + x4)
}
```

## A four-dimensional Normal example

We fit the joint tensor with the direct Normal fitter and with boosting, then compare these fits with additive local-scoring and boosting models. The joint boost starts from an initial GeDS learner (`initial_learner = TRUE`). Training uses a complete grid with seven values per coordinate (2,401 observations), which also allows efficient tensor-grid coefficient computation.

```{r fit-normal, results='hide'}
values <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 7)
train <- expand.grid(
  x1 = values, x2 = values,
  x3 = values, x4 = values
)

set.seed(123)
train$truth <- with(train, wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4))
train$y <- train$truth + rnorm(nrow(train), sd = 0.15)

fit_ngeds <- NGeDS(
  y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train
)

fit_boost_joint <- NGeDSboost(
  y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train,
  initial_learner = TRUE
)

fit_gam <- NGeDSgam(
  y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train
)

fit_boost_additive <- NGeDSboost(
  y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train
)
```

The localized peaks in `x1` and `x2` interact with all four coordinates. The selected linear knots and averaged quadratic and cubic knots are:

```{r}
fit_ngeds$linear.intknots
fit_ngeds$quadratic.intknots
fit_ngeds$cubic.intknots
```

To isolate the contribution of knot insertion, we compare the quadratic GeDS fit (`n = 3`, degree 2) with a quadratic tensor without internal knots. Products of quadratic polynomials include every combination of powers 0, 1 and 2 across the four coordinates. Both fits have the same degree in each coordinate. Test observations are sampled independently of the training grid.

```{r}
no_knot_tensor <- lm(
  y ~ poly(x1, 2, raw = TRUE) *
    poly(x2, 2, raw = TRUE) *
    poly(x3, 2, raw = TRUE) *
    poly(x4, 2, raw = TRUE),
  data = train
)
set.seed(321)
test <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(1000), x2 = runif(1000),
  x3 = runif(1000), x4 = runif(1000)
)
test$truth <- with(test, wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4))

round(c(
  `No internal knots` = mean((test$truth - predict(no_knot_tensor, test))^2),
  `NGeDS joint` = mean((test$truth - predict(fit_ngeds, test, n = 3))^2),
  `NGeDSboost joint` = mean((test$truth - predict(fit_boost_joint, test, n = 3))^2),
  `NGeDSgam additive` = mean((test$truth - predict(fit_gam, test, n = 3))^2),
  `NGeDSboost additive` = mean((test$truth - predict(fit_boost_additive, test, n = 3))^2)
), 3)
```

The response depends on products of the coordinates: an additive model cannot represent it exactly. For the surface slices, `x3` and `x4` are fixed at 0.25 while `x1` and `x2` vary over a grid.

```{r four-dimensional-surface, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2}
grid_values <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 45)
surface_data <- expand.grid(
  x1 = grid_values, x2 = grid_values,
  x3 = 0.25, x4 = 0.25
)

truth_surface <- matrix(
  with(surface_data, wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4)),
  nrow = length(grid_values)
)
fitted_surface <- matrix(
  predict(fit_ngeds, surface_data, n = 3),
  nrow = length(grid_values)
)

surface_colours <- hcl.colors(30, "Blue-Red 3")
surface_limits <- range(truth_surface, fitted_surface, finite = TRUE)
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
image(grid_values, grid_values, truth_surface,
      col = surface_colours, zlim = surface_limits, xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "True 4D surface slice")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, truth_surface, add = TRUE,
        drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
image(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_surface,
      col = surface_colours, zlim = surface_limits, xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "Quadratic NGeDS slice")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_surface, add = TRUE,
        drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
par(old_par)
```

The next plot follows a path through the four-dimensional space: `x1` and `x2` vary together, while `x3` and `x4` are fixed. This reveals the interaction as a curve along the path.

```{r four-dimensional-curves, fig.height=8}
slice_data <- data.frame(
  x1 = seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 250),
  x2 = seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 250), x3 = 0.25, x4 = 0.25
)
slice_fits <- cbind(
  Truth = with(slice_data, wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4)),
  `NGeDS joint` = predict(fit_ngeds, slice_data, n = 3),
  `NGeDSboost joint` = predict(fit_boost_joint, slice_data, n = 3),
  `NGeDSgam additive` = predict(fit_gam, slice_data, n = 3),
  `NGeDSboost additive` = predict(fit_boost_additive, slice_data, n = 3)
)

old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
layout(matrix(1:2, ncol = 1), heights = c(5, 2))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
matplot(
  slice_data$x1,
  slice_fits,
  type = "l", lty = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4), lwd = c(3, 2, 2, 2, 2),
  col = c("grey20", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"),
  ylim = range(slice_fits, finite = TRUE),
  xlab = "x1 = x2", ylab = "True / fitted mean",
  main = "Interaction path: x1 = x2, x3 = x4 = 0.25"
)
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend(
  "center", ncol = 2, cex = 0.85,
  c("Truth", "NGeDS joint (degree 2)", "NGeDSboost joint (degree 2)",
    "NGeDSgam additive (degree 2)", "NGeDSboost additive (degree 2)"),
  lty = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4), lwd = c(3, 2, 2, 2, 2),
  col = c("grey20", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"),
  bty = "n"
)
layout(1)
par(old_par)
```

The y-axis includes every fitted curve on the original response scale.

## Repeated test-sample comparison

We repeat the experiment with four noise realizations on the same training grid and compare quadratic test mean squared errors against the known function. All models use the same independent test sample. The additive models cannot represent the four-way interaction exactly.

```{r gaussian-boxplots, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, results='hide'}
set.seed(123)
n_repetitions <- 4
normal_results <- vector("list", n_repetitions)

for (b in seq_len(n_repetitions)) {
  train_b <- train
  train_b$y <- train_b$truth + rnorm(nrow(train_b), sd = 0.15)
  test_b <- test

  ngeds_b <- NGeDS(
    y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train_b
  )
  boost_joint_b <- NGeDSboost(
    y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train_b,
    initial_learner = TRUE
  )
  gam_b <- NGeDSgam(
    y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train_b
  )
  boost_additive_b <- NGeDSboost(
    y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train_b
  )

  normal_results[[b]] <- c(
    "NGeDS joint (degree 2)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(ngeds_b, test_b, n = 3))^2),
    "NGeDSboost joint (degree 2)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(boost_joint_b, test_b, n = 3))^2),
    "NGeDSgam additive (degree 2)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(gam_b, test_b, n = 3))^2),
    "NGeDSboost additive (degree 2)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(boost_additive_b, test_b, n = 3))^2)
  )
}

normal_mse <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, normal_results))
old_par <- par(mar = c(10, 4, 3, 1))
boxplot(
  normal_mse, names = rep("", 4), xaxt = "n", log = "y",
  col = c("#0072B2", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"),
  ylab = "Test MSE (log scale)", cex.axis = 0.85,
  main = "Four-dimensional Gaussian experiment"
)
stripchart(normal_mse, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("grey15", 0.65), add = TRUE)
mtext(c("NGeDS joint\ndegree 2", "Boost joint\ndegree 2",
        "GAM additive\ndegree 2", "Boost additive\ndegree 2"),
      side = 1, at = 1:4, line = 3.5, cex = 0.75)
par(old_par)

round(vapply(normal_mse, median, numeric(1)), 3)
```

The additive models can capture marginal patterns, but not the four-way interaction itself. The test MSE comparison therefore shows what the joint tensor adds beyond separate univariate smoothers.

The joint boosting fit uses `initial_learner = TRUE` as specified above. The common boxplot uses a log scale so that all four test-error distributions can be compared on the same axes.

## A four-dimensional generalized-response example

The same tensor syntax is available in `GGeDS`. For the Poisson example, we use
a broader four-dimensional peak that the default knot-insertion procedure can
resolve. The conditional mean depends jointly on all four coordinates. We show
the linear Stage A tensor fit, whose selected internal knots describe the peak.

```{r poisson-fit, results='hide'}
poisson_mean <- function(x1, x2, x3, x4) {
  peak <- exp(-6 * ((x1 - 0.5)^2 + (x2 - 0.5)^2 +
                     (x3 - 0.5)^2 + (x4 - 0.5)^2))
  exp(4 + 2 * peak)
}

set.seed(123)
poisson_train <- train
poisson_train$mu <- with(poisson_train, poisson_mean(x1, x2, x3, x4))
poisson_train$count <- rpois(nrow(poisson_train), poisson_train$mu)

fit_ggeds <- GGeDS(
  count ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4),
  family = poisson(), data = poisson_train
)
```

The selected linear internal knots are:

```{r}
fit_ggeds$linear.intknots
```

The response-scale fitted surface can again be displayed as a two-dimensional
slice, using a common colour scale and contour levels for the true and fitted means.

```{r poisson-surface, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2}
poisson_surface_data <- surface_data
true_mean_surface <- with(
  poisson_surface_data,
  matrix(poisson_mean(x1, x2, x3, x4),
         nrow = length(grid_values))
)
fitted_mean_surface <- matrix(
  predict(fit_ggeds, poisson_surface_data, n = 2),
  nrow = length(grid_values)
)

mean_limits <- range(true_mean_surface, fitted_mean_surface, finite = TRUE)
mean_contours <- pretty(mean_limits, n = 6)
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
image(grid_values, grid_values, true_mean_surface,
      col = hcl.colors(30, "YlOrRd"), zlim = mean_limits,
      xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "True Poisson mean")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, true_mean_surface, add = TRUE,
        levels = mean_contours, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
image(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_mean_surface,
      col = hcl.colors(30, "YlOrRd"), zlim = mean_limits,
      xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "Linear GGeDS fitted mean")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_mean_surface, add = TRUE,
        levels = mean_contours, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
par(old_par)
```

For a small repeated comparison, we use an ordinary Poisson GLM with linear main effects as a familiar benchmark. Thus, `count ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4` is compared with the flexible joint tensor `count ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4)`. The loss is the mean Poisson deviance relative to the true conditional mean.

```{r poisson-boxplots, fig.height=4.5, results='hide'}
set.seed(123)
poisson_results <- vector("list", n_repetitions)

for (b in seq_len(n_repetitions)) {
  train_b <- poisson_train
  train_b$count <- rpois(nrow(train_b), train_b$mu)
  test_b <- test
  test_b$mu <- with(test_b, poisson_mean(x1, x2, x3, x4))

  ggeds_b <- GGeDS(
    count ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4),
    family = poisson(), data = train_b
  )
  fitted_mean <- predict(ggeds_b, test_b, n = 2)
  glm_b <- glm(
    count ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4,
    family = poisson(), data = train_b
  )
  glm_mean <- predict(glm_b, test_b, type = "response")

  poisson_results[[b]] <- c(
    "Linear Poisson GLM" = mean(poisson()$dev.resids(test_b$mu, glm_mean, 1)),
    "GGeDS joint tensor (degree 1)" = mean(poisson()$dev.resids(test_b$mu, fitted_mean, 1))
  )
}

poisson_deviance <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, poisson_results))
old_par <- par(mar = c(7, 4, 3, 1))
boxplot(
  poisson_deviance,
  names = c("Linear\nPoisson GLM", "GGeDS joint\ndegree 1"),
  col = c("grey75", "#CC79A7"),
  ylab = "Mean Poisson deviance", cex.axis = 0.85,
  main = "Four-dimensional Poisson experiment"
)
stripchart(poisson_deviance, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("grey15", 0.65), add = TRUE)
par(old_par)

round(vapply(poisson_deviance, median, numeric(1)), 3)
```

Here the joint `GGeDS` tensor is compared with a model that uses all four covariates, but restricts each of their effects to be linear.

## Moving to five dimensions

Nothing in the formula changes when a fifth coordinate is added. Here two peaks in `x1` have an amplitude that depends jointly on all four remaining coordinates. This is a five-way interaction, although curvature is concentrated in `x1`: the other four directions are linear. A tensor grid gives seven training values in the curved direction and four in each remaining direction, for 1,792 observations.

```{r five-dimensional-fit, results='hide'}
wiggly5 <- function(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5) {
  g <- function(x) {
    exp(-50 * (x - 0.3)^2) + 0.6 * exp(-80 * (x - 0.75)^2)
  }
  3 * g(x1) * (0.5 + x2) * (0.5 + x3) *
    (0.5 + x4) * (0.5 + x5)
}

values5 <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 7)
other_values <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 4)
train5 <- expand.grid(
  x1 = values5, x2 = other_values, x3 = other_values,
  x4 = other_values, x5 = other_values
)
set.seed(123)
train5$truth <- with(train5, wiggly5(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5))
train5$y <- train5$truth + rnorm(nrow(train5), sd = 0.15)

fit5 <- NGeDS(
  y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5), data = train5
)
```

The selected linear internal knot counts in this five-dimensional example are:

```{r}
lengths(fit5$linear.intknots)
```

We compare the linear and quadratic GeDS fits using an independent test sample and the true generating function. A linear tensor without internal knots provides a reference for the improvement due to adaptive knot insertion in the linear fit.

```{r five-dimensional-mse}
no_knot5 <- lm(y ~ x1 * x2 * x3 * x4 * x5, data = train5)

set.seed(321)
test5 <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(1000), x2 = runif(1000), x3 = runif(1000),
  x4 = runif(1000), x5 = runif(1000)
)
test5$truth <- with(test5, wiggly5(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5))

round(c(
  `No internal knots (degree 1)` =
    mean((test5$truth - predict(no_knot5, test5))^2),
  `NGeDS joint (degree 1)` =
    mean((test5$truth - predict(fit5, test5, n = 2))^2),
  `NGeDS joint (degree 2)` =
    mean((test5$truth - predict(fit5, test5, n = 3))^2)
), 3)
```

Two slices show the linear and quadratic fits at different interaction amplitudes. All curves are plotted on their original response scale, without vertical alignment.

```{r five-dimensional-slice, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE),
       heights = c(5, 1))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (level in c(0.25, 0.75)) {
  slice5 <- data.frame(
    x1 = seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 250),
    x2 = level, x3 = level, x4 = level, x5 = level
  )
  curves5 <- cbind(
    Truth = with(slice5, wiggly5(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5)),
    Linear = predict(fit5, slice5, n = 2),
    Quadratic = predict(fit5, slice5, n = 3)
  )
  matplot(
    slice5$x1, curves5, type = "l",
    lty = c(1, 2, 1), lwd = c(3, 2, 2),
    col = c("grey20", "#0072B2", "#009E73"),
    ylim = range(curves5, finite = TRUE),
    xlab = "x1", ylab = "True / fitted mean",
    main = paste("x2 = x3 = x4 = x5 =", level)
  )
}

par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend(
  "center", ncol = 3, cex = 0.85,
  legend = c("Truth", "NGeDS linear (degree 1)",
             "NGeDS quadratic (degree 2)"),
  lty = c(1, 2, 1), lwd = c(3, 2, 2),
  col = c("grey20", "#0072B2", "#009E73"), bty = "n"
)
layout(1)
par(old_par)
```

The same syntax extends to further dimensions, but tensor-product basis sizes grow multiplicatively. In practice, higher-dimensional models should therefore be accompanied by careful out-of-sample validation and by plots of informative low-dimensional slices such as those above.
